To talk about free time and make plans: “Hai să…!”
Thursday, at the office. Ana asks Nora what she is doing at the weekend. Ana wants to go to the Turda Gorge, a spectacular canyon 30 kilometres from Cluj.
Nora, what are you doing on Saturday? Let’s go to the Turda Gorge!
A canyon between two mountains, with a river and very high cliffs. It’s the most beautiful place around Cluj.
Sounds wonderful! But what will the weather be like? The weather here changes very quickly.
Let me look on my phone… Saturday is sunny, twenty-two degrees. Sunday it rains.
Perfect, Saturday then. It’s warmer than in Sweden right now! In Gothenburg in October it’s ten degrees and it always rains.
Can you hike in the mountains? The trail isn’t very hard, but it’s long: three hours.
Of course I can. In Sweden we spend a lot of time in nature. But I don’t have hiking boots.
No problem, you can take my sister’s boots. What shoe size are you?
Same as her! Then we leave on Saturday at eight. Take a jacket, it’s cold in the mountains in the morning.
And Radu? Can he come too?
Radu? Hm… Of course he can. If he knows how to wake up at seven!
the gorge (here: a narrow pass between mountains)
“din jurul” = around, in the area of
“stai să…” = wait while I…, let me…
“ce număr porți?” = what shoe size are you?
“să vină” = the form of “a veni” after “să” (he)
“iarnă” is read “yar-nă”, with a short gliding “i” in one syllable with the “a”.
“ploaie” has three linked vowel sounds: “ploa-ie”. “oa” is a single syllable.
“ști” is pronounced “shti”. “știu” = “shtiu”, one syllable. Don’t confuse “știu” (I know) with “știi” (you know).
“ge” is read as in Italian (“gelato”), like “je” in English “jet”: “nin-ge”.
For the weather, Romanian mostly uses “e” (it is) + adjective, or impersonal verbs (with no subject).
the sky is clear / covered with clouds
you can’t see well because of the fog
How many degrees is it outside?
Are you hot? (do you feel hot?)
When you talk about what you feel, you say “mi-e frig / mi-e cald” (with the dative), not “sunt frig”.
Months are written with a small letter. For “in (the month of)…” you use “în”: “în octombrie”, “în mai”.
In summer I go to the seaside. (every summer)

“Cel mai” agrees with the noun: “cel mai înalt munte” (the highest mountain), “cea mai înaltă stâncă” (the highest cliff), “cei mai buni prieteni” (the best friends), “cele mai frumoase locuri” (the most beautiful places).
For intensity, Romanians also use “tare” or “extrem de”: “E tare frumos!” (It’s really beautiful!), “E extrem de cald!” (It’s extremely hot!).
For the superlative you don’t say “mai bun decât” (better than) but “cel mai bun” (the best). “Bine” (well) → “mai bine” (better), “cel mai bine” (best).
In English both can be “can”, but in Romanian they are different:
a fact, or a skill you have learned
Can you ski today? (is it possible today?)
“A putea” can also be followed by the infinitive without “să”: “Pot veni” = “Pot să vin” (I can come). Both are correct.
Do you want to go out tonight?
“Hai!” is used a lot: “Hai, repede!” (Come on, quickly!), “Hai acasă!” (Let’s go home!), “Hai să mâncăm!” (Let’s eat!). In the plural: “Haideți!”.

It’s Friday evening. Nora’s room is in chaos. On my red rug there are a jacket, a jumper, a bottle of water, a map, three bananas and a camera. I’m sitting on the map. It’s the best place in the room.
“Mițu, please, I need the map,” says Nora. I don’t move. The map is warm. Nora sighs and pulls the map out from under me, very slowly.
Mrs Pop comes in with a box. “I’ve made you some sandwiches for tomorrow. With cheese and tomatoes. In the mountains you’re always hungry, more than at home.”
“Thank you, Mrs Pop! But there are too many. There are only three of us.”
“Three?” asks Mrs Pop, raising an eyebrow. “Who else is coming, apart from you and Ana?”
Nora blushes a little. “Radu. If he wakes up in time.”
Mrs Pop smiles, but says nothing. She puts two more sandwiches in the box. “Radu eats for two,” she says. “I know, he’s my grandson.”
Then she looks out of the window. “You should know that at the Turda Gorge the weather changes quickly. In the morning it’s cold, at noon it’s hot, and in the evening the wind blows. Take a hat too.”
“A hat? In October?” Nora laughs. “Mrs Pop, I’m from Sweden. Back home, in October, it’s much colder than here.”
“All right, all right,” says Mrs Pop. “But you don’t know how cold it can get in our mountains. Listen to an old teacher.”
Nora puts the hat in the rucksack. I look at the rucksack. It’s big, it’s soft and it’s open.
When Nora goes out of the room to brush her teeth, I climb into the rucksack. I make myself small, very small, between the jumper and the hat. It’s the cosiest place in the whole house.
Five minutes later, Nora comes back and wants to close the rucksack. “Mițu!” she shouts. “No! You can’t come to the mountains!”
I know I can’t. But a tomcat is allowed to try.
the rucksack (bag you carry on your back)
“cât doi” = as much as two people
teeth (“să se spele pe dinți” = to brush her teeth)
“să închidă” = the form of “a închide” after “să”

The weather forecast for the weekend
Good evening! Here is the weather forecast for this weekend in Transylvania.
On Saturday the weather will be fine. In the morning it will be cool, at eight degrees, but by noon temperatures will rise to twenty-two degrees.
The sky will be clear for most of the day. In the evening, in the mountains, the wind will blow.
On Sunday the weather turns bad. Clouds will come from the west and it will rain across the whole region.
In Cluj it will be only fourteen degrees. On the mountain peaks, above two thousand metres, it may snow.
Our advice: on Saturday go out into nature, and on Sunday stay at home with a good book and a hot tea.
Transylvania (region in the centre of Romania)
“vor urca” = future of “a urca” (they will rise)
“va ploua” = future of “a ploua” (it will rain)
“să ningă” = the form of “a ninge” after “să”
On Sunday it’s best to stay at home with a book.
